h1: Yarn Weight Chart Explained: From Lace to Jumbo
lede: Yarn weight is the single most important number on a yarn label — and the most misunderstood. This guide walks you through the standard 0–7 scale, what each weight feels like, and how thickness changes the yardage your project needs.
meta_desc: Confused by yarn weights 0 to 7? This complete yarn weight chart explains lace through jumbo thickness, yards per 100g, and which projects each weight suits.

sections.h2: What does yarn weight actually mean?
sections.html:
Yarn weight has nothing to do with how heavy a skein is on a scale. It is the thickness of the strand, standardized by the Craft Yarn Council on a scale from 0 (lace) to 7 (jumbo). A 100 g skein of lace weight and a 100 g skein of super bulky weigh exactly the same — but the lace skein holds roughly ten times more yardage.

This matters because patterns are written for a specific thickness. Substitute a thicker or thinner yarn and your finished piece comes out a different size, with a different drape — unless you do the yardage math. Our yarn yardage calculator handles that conversion for you: pick your project and the new yarn weight, and it recalculates the yardage instantly.

Here is the full standard scale with typical yardage per 100 g and the projects each weight is best for:

WeightCategoryYards / 100 gBest for
0Lace600–800Shawls, fine doilies
1Super fine / Fingering400–460Socks, lightweight shawls
2Fine / Sport300–350Baby garments, light sweaters
3Light / DK250–300Sweaters, baby blankets
4Medium / Worsted200–230Sweaters, blankets, scarves
5Bulky100–130Quick knits, chunky blankets
6Super bulky60–80Arm knitting, rugs
7Jumbo30–50Extreme chunky blankets

Note that different brands vary, so always check the number printed on your own ball band — our calculator lets you enter the exact yardage per skein. If you are still learning to decode labels, see how to read a yarn label.

sections.h2: How yarn weight changes your yardage
sections.html:
Thicker yarn covers more area per yard, so you need fewer total yards — but each skein also contains fewer yards. That is why a throw blanket takes about 2,200 yards in worsted but only 1,400 yards in super bulky: the super-bulky version is much heavier and uses far more skeins by weight.

Rule of thumb: when you move one weight thicker, total yardage drops by roughly 15–20%. Going thinner does the reverse. The calculator's built-in table already accounts for this per project, so you don't have to estimate by hand.

sections.h2: Choosing the right weight for your project
sections.html: Match the weight to the job. Garments that drape (sweaters, shawls) work best in fingering through worsted. Hard-wearing items (rugs, bags) want bulky and up. Baby items usually sit in sport to worsted — soft and washable beats everything else. And remember that crochet eats about 25–30% more yarn than knitting for the same size; read crochet vs knitting: which uses more yarn before you buy.

sections.h2: Yarn weight vs. WPI (wraps per inch)
sections.html:
WPI — wraps per inch — is the old-school way to measure thickness: wrap the yarn around a ruler and count how many wraps fit in one inch. Lace is 30+ WPI, fingering 19–22, DK 15–18, worsted 12–14, bulky 9–11. The Craft Yarn Council scale replaced WPI on modern labels, but spinners and vintage-pattern users still speak WPI — if a vintage pattern says “18 WPI”, that is modern DK.

WPI is also handy for mystery skeins with no label: wrap, count, and match to the chart above. Then sanity-check with the calculator — pick your project, enter the weight you estimated, and compare the yardage against what you actually have on hand.

h1: How to Read a Yarn Label: Yardage, Weight, Fiber & More
lede: That paper band around your skein is a cheat sheet: it tells you exactly how much yarn you have, what it's made of, and what it can become. Here's how to decode every line.
meta_desc: Learn how to read a yarn label like a pro: yardage, yarn weight, fiber content, dye lot, gauge, and care symbols — everything the ball band tells you.

sections.h2: The numbers that matter most: yardage and weight
sections.html:
Every label lists two key figures: the net weight (often 50 g or 100 g) and the yardage or meterage (e.g., 220 yds / 201 m). Yardage is what patterns and calculators actually use — plug the yardage per skein into the yarn yardage calculator for an exact skein count instead of relying on generic charts.

You'll also see the yarn weight category (0–7) and often a recommended hook or needle size. If the weight number is missing, our yarn weight chart helps you estimate it from the yardage per 100 g.

sections.h2: Fiber content: what your yarn is made of
sections.html: Labels list fibers by percentage — 100% acrylic, 75% wool / 25% nylon, and so on. Fiber drives everything: warmth, drape, washability, and price. Wool is warm and elastic but often hand-wash; acrylic is cheap, washable, and great for baby blankets; cotton is breathable and sturdy but heavy and inelastic — better for market bags than for stretchy socks.

sections.h2: Dye lot: the number that saves your project
sections.html: The dye lot is the batch your skein was dyed in. Colors can shift slightly between lots — enough to show as a visible stripe in a large piece. Always buy all the yarn for one project, plus your buffer, from the same dye lot. This is one reason we recommend the 10% buffer rule: running out mid-project and finding the lot is gone is a classic heartbreak.

The little knitted square shows gauge: how many stitches and rows make 4 inches (10 cm) with the recommended needles. Your own gauge will differ — swatch before substituting yarn (see how to substitute yarn in a pattern). Care symbols tell you whether the yarn is machine washable; for anything baby-related, washable is non-negotiable.

sections.h2: Putting it all together: a worked example
sections.html:
Say your label reads: 100 g, 220 yds, 100% acrylic, medium (4), dye lot 1234, gauge 18 sts × 24 rows = 4 in on US 8. Translation: you hold 220 yards of washable medium-weight yarn. A baby blanket in this yarn needs about 1,050 yards — that is 5 skeins (1,050 ÷ 220 = 4.8, round up), and the buffer rule makes it 6. Buy all six from dye lot 1234.

The gauge line tells you the designer's tension. If your swatch gives 20 stitches per 4 inches instead of 18, your blanket comes out smaller — size up your needles or add stitches. Keep the labels until the project is finished and washed: if you run short, the dye lot and exact product name are your only hope of matching the color.

h1: Fingering vs DK vs Worsted: Which Yarn Weight to Choose
lede: These three weights cover most knitting and crochet projects — but they behave very differently. Here's how fingering, DK, and worsted compare on thickness, yardage, drape, and speed, and which one your project actually wants.
meta_desc: Fingering vs DK vs worsted yarn: compare thickness, yardage per 100g, drape, and speed. Find the right weight for sweaters, blankets, and accessories.

sections.html: Fingering (1) is thin and light at 400–460 yards per 100 g — made for socks, shawls, and fine garments. DK (3), double-knitting, sits in the middle at 250–300 yards per 100 g — the all-rounder for sweaters and baby knits. Worsted (4) is the medium workhorse at 200–230 yards per 100 g — fast to work and forgiving for beginners. For the full 0–7 scale, see the yarn weight chart.

Fingering gives you beautiful drape and stitch definition, which is why it dominates socks and shawls. The trade-off is time: a fingering-weight sweater needs around 2,000 yards and many more stitches than the same sweater in worsted. Choose it when drape matters more than speed.

DK is the most popular garment weight for a reason: it drapes better than worsted, works up faster than fingering, and shows cables and texture beautifully. Most commercial sweater patterns are written for DK. A DK baby sweater takes roughly 700 yards; check the exact number for your size in the yardage calculator.

Worsted is the beginner's best friend — stitches are easy to see, mistakes are easy to fix, and projects fly. It is the default for scarves, hats, and cozy throw blankets. The downside is bulk: worsted garments are warmer and heavier, with less elegant drape than DK or fingering.

sections.h2: So which one for your project?
sections.html: Pick fingering for drape and detail, DK for garments you will wear often, and worsted for speed, warmth, and learning. Whatever you choose, confirm the skein count before buying — yarn weight changes both total yardage and yards per skein, and the calculator does that conversion in one step. And if a pattern calls for one weight but your stash has another, read how to substitute yarn in a pattern first.

Sport (2) is DK's lighter sibling — lovely for baby sweaters and light spring garments. Bulky (5) and super bulky (6) are the speed demons: a hat in super bulky can take under two hours, and a throw blanket flies by. Lace (0) belongs almost entirely to shawls. As a beginner, start with worsted, graduate to DK for your first fitted garment, and save fingering for when your tension is even.

When in doubt, check the pattern's recommended weight first — designers choose it for drape and fabric behavior, not just speed.

h1: How to Substitute Yarn in a Pattern (Yardage Math Made Simple)
lede: Found the perfect pattern but not the exact yarn? You don't need the pattern's yarn — you need its yardage. Here's the step-by-step math to substitute any yarn confidently.
meta_desc: How to substitute yarn in any knitting or crochet pattern: step-by-step yardage math, gauge swatch rules, and a worked example so you never run short on yarn.

sections.h2: Why patterns name a specific yarn
sections.html: Patterns list a yarn so you can match the designer's gauge and drape — but the critical number is the total yardage, not the brand. If you can compute total yards and match gauge, almost any yarn works. Start by learning to read a yarn label so you can pull the right numbers off the ball band.

sections.h2: Step 1: find the pattern's total yardage
sections.html: Multiply the number of skeins the pattern calls for by the yardage per skein of the pattern's yarn. Example: a pattern needs 6 skeins of a yarn with 220 yards per skein — that's 1,320 yards total. If the pattern only gives grams, convert using the yarn weight chart: worsted runs about 220 yards per 100 g.

sections.h2: Step 2: convert to your yarn's skeins
sections.html: Divide the total yards by the yardage per skein of your yarn, then round up and add a buffer. Same example with a 150-yard-per-skein substitute: 1,320 ÷ 150 = 8.8 → 9 skeins, plus one extra for safety (see the 10% buffer rule). The yarn yardage calculator does this division for every project and weight automatically.

Math gets you the right amount; a swatch gets you the right size. Knit or crochet a 4-inch square in your substitute yarn, wash and block it the way you will treat the finished piece, then measure. If your stitch count doesn't match the pattern, change hook or needle size — and recheck the yardage, because tighter or looser gauge changes how much yarn you consume.

sections.h2: Watch the fiber, not just the numbers
sections.html: Two yarns can match on weight and still behave differently: cotton stretches less than wool, acrylic drapes differently than alpaca. For structured pieces like a sweater or cardigan, stay in the same fiber family when you can. For blankets and scarves, fiber is more forgiving — drape differences just become design features.

Matching grams instead of yards. 200 g of lace holds roughly 1,400 yards; 200 g of super bulky holds about 140. Always substitute by yardage. Ignoring fiber behavior. A wool sweater pattern worked in cotton will grow longer and sag — fibers have memory, or they don't. Skipping the swatch. Ten minutes now beats frogging ten hours later. Forgetting the buffer. Substitution adds uncertainty, so bump your buffer to 15% (see the buffer rule). Get these four right and substitutions stop being scary.

h1: Best Yarn for Baby Blankets: Soft, Safe & Washable Picks
lede: A baby blanket gets chewed, dragged, and washed weekly — so the best yarn is soft against newborn skin, machine washable, and free of scratchy fibers. Here are the fibers and weights that actually work.
meta_desc: Best yarn for baby blankets: the softest washable fibers, safe picks for newborns, ideal weights, yardage needs, and one-dye-lot buying tips. Start here.

sections.h2: What matters most in a baby yarn
sections.html: Three non-negotiables: softness (test it against your cheek, not your hand), washability (machine wash and dry, because it will be washed constantly), and safety (no novelty yarns with long eyelash fibers a baby could pull loose and chew). Everything else — color, price, brand — comes second.

sections.h2: The best fibers for baby blankets
sections.html: Acrylic is the default for good reason: soft modern acrylics are inexpensive, fully washable, and come in every color. Look for “baby” or “soft” lines rather than the cheapest craft-store skeins. Superwash wool blends (wool treated to survive the washing machine, often blended with acrylic or nylon) are warmer and springier — lovely for heirloom blankets. Cotton blends are breathable and great for warm climates, but pure cotton is heavy and inelastic; a cotton-acrylic blend gives you softness without the weight. Avoid mohair, alpaca, and any yarn labeled hand-wash only.

Sport (2), DK (3), and worsted (4) cover nearly all baby blankets. DK is the sweet spot — soft drape, reasonable speed, and not too bulky to fold into a stroller. Bulky works for a quick gift blanket but makes a stiff, heavy fabric. Check the per-weight numbers on our baby blanket yardage page: a standard 30×36-inch blanket needs about 1,150 yards in DK or 1,050 in worsted.

Use the yarn yardage calculator with your exact yarn's yardage per skein (from the label), then add the 10% buffer — and buy it all in one dye lot. For a typical baby blanket that means 5–6 skeins of worsted or DK. Buying one extra skein is cheap insurance against a discontinued colorway.

Pastels are classic, but modern baby blankets go bold — high-contrast patterns engage newborns' developing vision. Variegated yarns do the colorwork for you; just check the dye lot across all skeins. For texture, seed stitch or granny squares hide uneven tension, which makes them great beginner choices.

Finish with a simple single-crochet border to stop curling, weave in ends securely — babies pull at everything — and wash once before gifting. That first wash softens the fibers, confirms the colors don't bleed, and pre-shrinks everything so the new parents can toss it straight in their own machine.

A handwritten care card tucked in with the gift is a thoughtful extra: machine wash cold, tumble dry low.

h1: How Many Skeins Do You Need? The 10% Buffer Rule
lede: Every yarn estimate assumes average gauge, an average size, and average luck. Real projects are none of those. The 10% buffer rule is the simple habit that keeps you from running out of yarn one skein short of finished.
meta_desc: The 10% buffer rule for buying yarn, explained: why yardage estimates fall short, when to use 15–20% instead, and why dye lots make spare skeins essential.

sections.html: Yardage charts — including ours — are computed for average gauge and standard sizes. Your tension, stitch pattern, and finished dimensions all shift the real number. Cable work eats more yarn than stockinette; a tall wearer needs a longer sweater; crochet consumes roughly 25–30% more than knitting (see crochet vs knitting yarn usage). The estimate is the starting line, not the finish.

The rule in one sentence: buy 10% more yarn than the chart says, rounded up to whole skeins. Here is how it plays out in practice.

Example 1 — hat: the chart says 200 yards in worsted. 200 × 1.10 = 220. Your skeins hold 220 yards each → exactly 1 skein; buy 2 anyway, same dye lot. Example 2 — throw blanket: 2,200 yards worsted. 2,200 × 1.10 = 2,420 ÷ 220 = 11 skeins exactly → buy 12. Example 3 — substituting yarn: the pattern needs 1,320 yards; your yarn has 150 yards per skein. 1,320 × 1.15 (substitution = 15%) = 1,518 ÷ 150 = 10.1 → 11 skeins.

The calculator's buffer field runs this math live — set it to 10 for routine projects and 15 when substituting yarn or working from a guess.

Take the calculated yardage, add 10%, divide by your skein's yardage, and round up. Example: a scarf needs 350 yards in worsted. Add 10% → 385 yards. Your skeins hold 220 yards each → 1.75 → buy 2 skeins. The yarn yardage calculator has a buffer field built in — it defaults to 10% and does this arithmetic for you.

Use 15–20% when any of these apply: it's your first project in this stitch pattern, you're substituting yarn (recheck with our substitution guide), the project is large (a queen blanket at 15% is 690 extra yards — that's three skeins of insurance on a month-long project), or the colorway could be discontinued. Dye lots are the real reason buffers exist: yarn bought months later may not match.

Buffers leave you with partial skeins — that's a feature. Leftover worsted becomes hats and mittens; fingering scraps become striped socks; everything else becomes amigurumi. A planned surplus is always cheaper than a stalled project.

h1: Crochet vs Knitting: Which Uses More Yarn?
lede: Crochet wins — and not in a good way. For the same finished size, crochet typically consumes 25–30% more yarn than knitting. Here's why, and how to adjust your yardage math for whichever craft you do.
meta_desc: Does crochet use more yarn than knitting? Yes — about 25-30% more. Learn why stitch choice changes everything, and how to adjust yardage math for your craft.

sections.html: It comes down to stitch architecture. A knit stitch is a single interlocking loop; a crochet stitch is a taller, denser knot that wraps yarn around the hook multiple times. Double crochet, treble crochet, and textured stitches like bobbles and popcorns are the hungriest — a heavily textured crochet throw blanket can use 40% more yarn than its knit equivalent.

Planning from a knitting pattern or a generic chart? Multiply the yardage by 1.3 for crochet. A knit scarf at 350 yards becomes ~455 yards in crochet; a knit hat at 200 yards becomes ~260. Our project tables are built from knitting-style estimates, so apply the uplift to the calculator's result — or just set the buffer field to 30% when crocheting from a knit pattern.

Not all crochet is equal. Lacy, open stitches (filet, v-stitch, mesh) use less yarn than the 30% rule suggests; dense stitches (single crochet, waistcoat stitch, cables) use more. Tunisian crochet sits between knitting and crochet. If your pattern is stitch-heavy, treat the 30% as a floor and use the 10% buffer rule on top.

Knitting is the economical craft, but cable and colorwork knitting narrow the gap — stranded colorwork can approach crochet-level consumption. Either way, the habit is the same: calculate for your actual craft, verify against your yarn label's yardage, and buy from one dye lot.

Rarely — but it happens. Stranded colorwork carries floats of unused yarn across the back of the fabric, and brioche is famously yarn-hungry: a brioche cowl can use double the yarn of plain stockinette. Cables consume extra too. If your knitting involves any of these techniques, apply the same 30% uplift you would use for crochet.

sections.h2: Which craft is cheaper to start?
sections.html:
Knitting uses less yarn per project, but startup costs differ: knitting needs needle sets in multiple sizes, while crochet needs one hook per project. For a scarf, the yarn gap (350 vs ~455 yards) is about half a skein — a few dollars. Over a blanket, it widens to several skeins. Choose your craft for the fabric you want, not the yarn bill — then calculate honestly for the craft you are doing.

Whatever your craft, the fix is the same: measure honestly for what you are actually making, then buy the buffer.

lede: A temperature blanket records a year of weather in yarn — one row per day, colored by the day's high. It's a beautiful project and a serious yarn investment. Here's how to plan colors, yardage, and budget before you cast on.
meta_desc: Temperature blanket yarn planning guide: how many colors you need, full-year yardage math, and budget tips for 365 rows of weather in yarn. Start planning here.

sections.html: Pick a year (or start today), assign each temperature range a color, then work one row — or one motif — per day in that day's color. A full year is 365 rows. At a typical gauge, that makes a blanket roughly 70–80 inches long, which is why most makers use throw-blanket dimensions as their planning baseline.

Map your local climate into 8–12 temperature bands of 5–10°F each, one color per band. Check a year of historical highs for your city so no color goes unused — a band that never occurs is a wasted skein. Keep the palette cohesive (a gradient from cool blues to warm reds is classic), and buy all colors from the same yarn line so weight and washability match. Worsted (4) is the most common choice: fast enough for 365 rows, warm enough to matter.

Estimate per-row yardage from a swatch: work 10 rows, measure yarn used, divide by 10. A typical worsted row across a throw-width blanket uses 12–18 yards; 365 rows × 15 yards ≈ 5,500 yards total. Divide by your skein's yardage (say 220) → 25 skeins, then apply the 10% buffer → ~28 skeins. Split across colors by your climate: extreme bands need 1–2 skeins, middle bands need 4–6. Run each color through the yarn yardage calculator as its own mini-project.

Twenty-eight skeins is real money — watch for sales and buy the full palette upfront (dye lots matter across a year-long project). Simplify: use two-row stripes per week instead of daily rows, or make a baby-blanket-sized version for a single season. And weave in ends as you go. Future you will be grateful.

sections.h2: Picking your year and data source
sections.html:
Use a past year so you can work continuously — weather sites publish daily highs by city and date, and a year of history is easy to pull. A birth year, wedding year, or first year in a new home turns the blanket into a keepsake. Record daily highs (not averages) for the most dramatic color range, and decide your rule for missing data now: repeat the previous day's color rather than guessing.

Track spending per color as you go — temperature blankets are notorious budget creepers, because buying “just one more skein” twelve times adds up fast.
